newsitem.title: UK: New depression, anxiety drugs needed, experts say.
newsitem.headline: New depression, anxiety drugs needed, experts say.

text.p: New and better drugs against anxiety and depression are badly needed but probably will not be developed until the next century, experts told a conference here on Tuesday.
Scientists and pharmaceutical companies were homing in on the molecular basis for disorders ranging from bipolar disorder (commonly known as manic-depression) to recurrent brief depression.

Drugs used against anxiety ranged from lithium to chlorpromazine to imipramine, Dai Stephens, an experimental psychologist at the University of Sussex, told the conference on anxiety and depression, organised by IBC.
"It is perhaps to the shame of rational science that all of these drugs were discovered by serendipity," Stephens said.
Stephens said he hoped a "rational approach" would come up with more and better drugs.
"We need more effective anti-depressants," agreed Rodger Pinder of Akxo Nobel NV unit Organon.

"The need for alternatives to lithium and existing anti-depressants is well-recognised. A less toxic, more effective lithium mimetic is required, together with antidepressants which are more effective and faster in action while retaining the gains already made better tolerability and safety in overdose."

Pinder said research targets for such new drugs included selective NA and 5-HT re-uptake inhibitors -- an area ventured into by drugs such as fluoxetine, best known as Eli Lilley & Co's much-publicized Prozac and citalopram.
Reversible inhibitors of monoamine oxidase A (RIMAs) were also possible short-term objectives.

"More fundamental research towards true third-generation anti-depressants is concentrating upon events beyond the receptor at the level of G-proteins, second messengers, protein phosphorylation and gene transcription factors," Pinder added.
Hormones and genetic influences both offered possibilities, he said, but added: "True third-generation anti-depressants will not be available until well into the next century."
That depression was common and life-threatening was not in dispute, speakers told the conference.

Pinder cited a study that found nine percent of the male and 25 percent of the female population in Europe had been treated for depression by the age of 30. Recurrent brief depression affected about 10 percent of the population and did not respond to current drugs, he added.
Patrice Boyer of France's National Institute of Medical Research (INSERM) said World Health Organisation surveys had shown anxiety disorders were widely underdiagnosed.
